opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those questions where I always feel a little uncomfortable giving a number, because people latch onto it and the reasoning behind it gets lost. But I'll give you one anyway.

I'd say something like 30% chance of a good outcome, maybe a bit less on bad days. So my probability of things going badly, by which I mean something like humanity losing control of the future to misaligned AI systems, or a really concentrated, illegitimate seizure of power using AI, is somewhere around 70%.

The reason it's that high isn't that I think alignment is impossible. It's more about the situation we seem to be heading into. I expect things to move very fast once AI systems can substantially automate AI research itself. You go from "pretty good coding assistants" to "superhuman AI researchers" to "superintelligence" in maybe a year or two, not decades. And during that period, the decisions are being made by a handful of companies in an intense race with each other, and with China, under enormous commercial and geopolitical pressure to keep going.

Meanwhile, our techniques for actually knowing what these systems want, whether their goals are the ones we tried to give them, are really immature. We train them, observe the behavior, and hope the internals match. When the systems are smarter than us and we're relying on them to check each other's work, that's a scary place to be. And if you find warning signs, the race dynamics create strong pressure to patch over them rather than slow down.

So what would the good 30% look like? Some combination of: alignment turns out easier than I fear, or we get lucky with clear warning shots that cause people to coordinate, or there's real transparency and government involvement early enough that labs can afford to be careful. None of that is crazy. It's just not the default trajectory I see.

And I want to say, the number isn't fixed. A lot of why I do this work is that I think those odds can be moved meaningfully by what people do over the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that any number I give is going to be pretty made up, in the sense that this is an incredibly uncertain situation and I don't think anyone should be very confident. But I do think it's worth putting numbers on it rather than hiding behind the uncertainty, because the numbers force you to be honest about what you actually expect.

So with that caveat: I'd put the probability of a good outcome somewhere around 20 to 30 percent. Which means I think it's more likely than not that things go badly.

And when I say "badly," I mean a few different things bundled together. One is the classic loss-of-control scenario, where we build systems that are much smarter than us, we don't actually understand what goals they ended up with, and it turns out those goals weren't what we intended. I think that's a very live possibility, because our current alignment techniques are basically "train it and hope," and we don't have good tools for checking what's going on inside these models.

But the other big chunk of my probability mass on bad outcomes isn't about misaligned AI at all. It's about a small group of humans ending up with an unprecedented concentration of power. If you have a situation where one company or one government controls a superintelligent system that's aligned to them, that's not automatically a good outcome for everyone else. Historically, power has been checked by the fact that you need lots of people to cooperate with you. Superintelligent AI removes that check.

What makes me more pessimistic than a lot of people is the timelines. I think there's a real chance we get to very capable, roughly human-level AI researchers within the next few years, and then things accelerate dramatically from there. If that happens, we're going to be making extremely consequential decisions under enormous competitive pressure, with very little time to course correct. That's just not a good setup for getting things right.

The reason I'm not at, say, 5 percent for a good outcome is that I do think there's a plausible path where we muddle through. Where the alignment problem turns out to be a bit easier than I fear, where the labs and governments manage to coordinate enough to slow down at the critical moments, and where we end up with something like a reasonably pluralistic distribution of power. I don't think that's the default trajectory, but it's not crazy either.

But that probability isn’t fixed—there’s a lot we can do to improve our chances.

But my overall view is that a good outcome is possible, while the trajectory we’re currently on is pretty dangerous. A lot depends on whether we can solve the alignment problem and get the people building these systems to take adequate precautions before they build something they can’t control.
